opus-5.5.text:
I think there are really two different speeds you have to keep in mind. There's the speed at which the underlying capability improves, which I think is very fast; we keep seeing these models get better on a pretty predictable curve. Then there's the speed at which that capability actually gets absorbed into the economy, and that's slower and messier. People sometimes conflate the two in both directions. Some say "the models are so smart, the whole economy will transform next year," and others say "adoption is slow, so the technology must be overhyped." I think both are wrong.

When I look at what actually limits diffusion, a few things stand out. One is plain organizational inertia. A large enterprise, a bank or a pharma company, has procurement processes, security reviews, compliance requirements, and people whose jobs are structured around existing workflows. Even if the model can do the task today, it takes time for someone inside the company to figure out how to plug it in, convince their leadership, retrain people, and rebuild the process around it. That's not irrational. It's just how institutions work.

A second is the physical world. A lot of the economy isn't just information processing. If AI designs a better drug, you still have to run clinical trials, which take years and involve real patients. If it designs a better chip or a better factory, someone still has to build it. So there are these physical and biological clocks that don't speed up just because the intelligence got better. I've sometimes framed this as asking what the marginal returns to intelligence are in a given domain. In some areas intelligence is the bottleneck, and in others the bottleneck is experiments, materials, or human coordination.

The third is regulation and legitimacy, which I'd actually defend in part. Society needs time to decide how it wants to use this technology and to build trust in it. Healthcare, law, and government all have safeguards that exist for good reasons.

That said, I think diffusion will be faster than in past technological revolutions. Electricity took decades to reshape factories because you literally had to redesign the factory floor. AI is delivered through software, so you can drop it in where people already work. And the models themselves can help with adoption. They can help write the integration code, explain themselves to users, and adapt to workflows. Coding is the clearest example: adoption there has been extraordinarily fast, because developers are early adopters and the feedback loop is tight.

So my overall picture is something like this: very fast relative to any previous technology, but not instantaneous. There's a lag of maybe a few years between "the model can do it" and "the economy is doing it at scale," and that lag differs a lot by sector. I think that's actually important for the transition, because it gives society some time to adapt. But it's not a lot of time, and I don't think we should be complacent about it.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes rapid capability improvement from slower economic absorption and names organizational, physical, regulatory, and trust constraints.

r002.rationale: It says diffusion will be faster than in past technological revolutions.

r003.rationale: It describes enterprise adoption barriers and fast coding adoption, but does not compare large enterprises with individual developers or startups on ease of setup.

r004.rationale: It identifies procurement, security and compliance reviews, leadership buy-in, retraining, and workflow redesign as enterprise adoption obstacles.

r005.rationale: It says adoption is not instantaneous despite fast-improving models, but does not specifically discuss AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the limits are mostly not on the model side anymore. They're on the human and institutional side. And I'd break it into a few pieces.

The first is just that the world has a lot of friction in it. Even if you have a model that can do a task as well as a person, someone has to figure out that it can, trust that it can, wire it into whatever system they're using, deal with the legal and compliance questions, retrain the people around it. Every one of those steps takes months in a normal company. That's the thing people underestimate. Technology has always diffused slower than the capability itself would suggest. Electricity took decades to change how factories were laid out, not because the motors didn't work but because you had to rebuild the factory.

The second piece is that the places where the friction is lowest are the places where the work is already digital and the feedback loop is fast. That's why software is first. You write code, you run it, you know almost immediately whether it worked. There's no regulator, no physical object, no twelve-month procurement cycle. So you see adoption in coding that's just dramatically ahead of everything else. Then I'd expect things like customer support, parts of finance, parts of legal, where the inputs and outputs are text. Then the physical world, biology, manufacturing, where you're bottlenecked on experiments and on atoms rather than bits.

The third thing, and this is the one I think is underappreciated, is that the models themselves could compress that friction. If you have systems that can do the integration work, that can read the legacy codebase, that can fill out the compliance paperwork, that can run the pilot and write up the results, then a lot of what used to take a year of human effort starts to take weeks. So diffusion isn't a fixed constant. It's something the technology can act on. That's part of why I think the curve could be steeper than historical analogies would suggest, even though I think the historical analogies are right about the direction of the drag.

And then there's a fourth category that I don't think the models fix, which is just that some things are slow because we've decided they should be slow. Drug approval is slow on purpose. Changing how a hospital works is slow partly because people's lives are at stake. I don't think that goes away, and I'm not sure I'd want it to go away entirely. So you could end up in a world where the capability is very broad, the adoption in software and knowledge work is very fast, and the adoption in the regulated physical economy lags by years. That gap is going to create a lot of strange dynamics, and honestly I think it's where a lot of the policy conversation should be focused rather than on the models themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says diffusion is limited mostly by human and institutional friction rather than model capability.

r002.rationale: It says the diffusion curve could be steeper than historical analogies suggest.

r003.rationale: It says software adoption is ahead of other areas, but does not compare large enterprises with individual developers or startups.

r004.rationale: It lists company integration, compliance, and retraining steps, but does not clearly identify internal approval and coordination as a bottleneck.

r005.rationale: It says adoption takes time even when a model can perform a task as well as a person, but does not make the claim about AGI specifically.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish how quickly the technology gets better from how quickly people can actually put it to work. Those are related, but they’re not the same clock.

Imagine you have a model that can do a particular task extremely well. You still need to connect it to the company’s data, change the workflow, figure out how to check its work, and establish who’s responsible when something goes wrong. Sometimes the task is only one part of a larger process, and making that part essentially free doesn’t speed up the whole process very much.

So I’d expect diffusion to be very uneven. In software, you can have a fairly short loop: generate something, test it, see whether it works. In a setting where you need to build a factory, run an experiment, or get regulatory approval, there are constraints that intelligence alone doesn’t immediately remove.

But I also wouldn’t assume that historical rates of adoption give us a fixed speed limit. AI can help with some of the work required to adopt AI. If integration is expensive because someone needs to write a lot of custom software, well, that’s itself a task the technology may make much cheaper.

The question is which bottlenecks remain after that. Is it a shortage of intelligence, or is it trust, organizational change, physical infrastructure? I could imagine very rapid progress in capabilities alongside a much more staggered transformation of the economy. And even that staggered transformation could be quite fast by historical standards.

r001.rationale: The response names adoption constraints beyond model capability, including integration, workflow changes, trust, organizational change, and physical infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It says the transformation could be fast by historical standards, but presents that as a possibility rather than predicting that AI will diffuse faster than previous technologies.

r003.rationale: It does not compare adoption by large enterprises with adoption by individual developers or startups.

r004.rationale: It mentions workflow changes, responsibility, and organizational change, but does not clearly identify internal approval and coordination as adoption bottlenecks.

r005.rationale: It discusses capable models and persistent adoption constraints, but does not address AGI or state that even AGI would not make adoption instantaneous.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between how quickly the technology gets better and how quickly the world can absorb it. Those are related, but they’re not the same clock.

If you have a model that can do a task, that doesn’t immediately mean you can replace an entire workflow. You need to integrate it with the company’s systems, figure out how to check its work, and decide who’s responsible when something goes wrong. Often the task is embedded in a whole set of organizational processes that have to change.

And the constraints differ a lot by sector. With software, you can distribute something very quickly, and you can often test whether it works fairly quickly. In medicine, even if you could come up with a promising treatment much faster, you still have clinical trials, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. Intelligence can help with those things, but it doesn’t automatically eliminate the time they take.

The thing that makes me hesitant to just assume diffusion will be slow is that AI can help with diffusion itself. It can help write the integration code, train people, and redesign workflows. So some of the bottlenecks are things the technology can work on. Others involve physical processes, institutions, or trust, and those may be much harder to compress.

So I’d expect a very uneven picture: some areas changing extremely quickly, while in others there’s a substantial gap between what a model can demonstrate and what’s actually being used throughout the economy.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes model capability from the economy’s ability to absorb AI, citing integration, workflow, regulatory, and trust constraints.

r002.rationale: It describes uneven and potentially rapid diffusion but does not compare AI’s pace with that of previous technologies.

r003.rationale: It does not compare adoption by large enterprises with adoption by individual developers or startups.

r004.rationale: It mentions organizational processes and workflow changes, but does not clearly identify internal approval and coordination as an adoption bottleneck.

r005.rationale: It says capable models do not immediately replace workflows, but does not state that even AGI would not make economic adoption instantaneous.
